slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood  ·  Units: ng/L, ng/mL

What it is used for: Mainly to confirm whether a person is having, or recently had, a heart attack — the most common reason; it is usually done in the emergency department together with other heart tests such as an ECG. It is also used to diagnose and monitor unstable angina and to check the heart after surgery that could damage it (tested before and after so results can be compared).

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Ordered with symptoms of a heart attack: chest pain, heaviness or discomfort in the centre or left side of the chest; pain in one or both arms, the back, shoulders, neck, jaw or above the belly button; trouble breathing at rest or with light activity; nausea and vomiting; unusual tiredness; dizziness; heavy sweating for no reason; a rapid or irregular heartbeat. With such symptoms, emergency help should be called immediately.

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Troponin is a protein found in heart muscle cells. Normally blood levels are so low that only the most sensitive tests can measure them; when heart muscle is damaged, troponin leaks into the bloodstream and the level rises. Two types — troponin I and troponin T — can be measured, and a test measures either one.

In a heart attack, blood flow that brings oxygen to part of the heart muscle is suddenly blocked; without oxygen, heart muscle cells die and release troponin. The more damage, the more troponin is released, so the amount also helps estimate how much of the heart has been damaged.

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
bullets: High: Higher than normal troponin usually means some damage to the heart muscle; very high levels most often mean a heart attack. Whether a heart attack caused the damage is decided by the provider, who considers symptoms, medical history and other test results.

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
bullets: High: High troponin does not always mean a heart attack. It can also rise with unstable angina and other conditions that damage the heart: arrhythmia (especially a heartbeat that is too fast), heart failure, heart valve disease, myocarditis, heart surgery, long intense exercise such as a marathon, chest injuries, chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, sepsis and severe COVID-19. If the provider does not think a heart attack occurred, other tests may be done to find the cause.

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
bullets: High: Troponin can keep rising for about 24 hours after a heart attack begins. So with a high result it is usually measured two or more times over 24 hours: how fast the level rises and its peak help estimate how much heart muscle is damaged and how well the person may recover.

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: A blood sample is taken from a vein in the arm. No special preparation is needed.
Interferences: Biotin (vitamin B7) and supplements containing it can make troponin levels appear lower than they really are, so the provider ordering the test should be told about biotin use.

slides.title: Cardiac troponin (cTnI, cTnT)
bullets: Limitations: A single normal result is not enough: if the first result is normal, the test is usually repeated within the next 12 hours, because troponin usually does not rise until about 2–3 hours after a heart attack begins. Meanwhile, other tests and exams guide whether to start treatment right away. A normal troponin 12 hours after symptoms began means a heart attack is unlikely.

slides.title: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood  ·  Units: ng/mL, U/L

What it is used for: If the source of high or rising total CK is not clear, a more specific CK isoenzymes test may be ordered to find out whether the CK is coming from the muscles, the heart or the brain.

Blood enzyme tests used to check for a heart attack include troponin and creatine kinase (CK). The enzyme CK-MB is released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged, and high CK-MB levels can mean a heart attack has occurred.

slides.title: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Creatine kinase (CK) is an enzyme that helps make energy. Most CK is in skeletal muscles, some is in heart muscle and small amounts are in the brain; when muscle, heart or brain tissue is damaged, more CK leaks from the cells into the blood.
A CK isoenzymes test measures three types of CK: CK-MM is mostly linked to skeletal muscle, CK-MB to heart muscle and CK-BB to the brain (conditions affecting smooth muscle can also raise CK-BB).

slides.title: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB)
bullets: High: High CK-MB is most likely from damage to the heart muscle, often caused by a heart attack or inflammation of the heart muscle (myocarditis). But other conditions can also raise CK-MB, such as a blood clot in the lung, heart surgery, congestive heart failure, hypothyroidism and kidney failure.

slides.title: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for CK testing, but the provider may ask you to avoid intense exercise and alcohol for a few days before the test to help make sure results are accurate.
Limitations: In certain cases a CK test may help diagnose a heart attack, but a troponin test is used more often because it is better at finding heart muscle damage from a heart attack.
To diagnose the cause of high CK, other tests may be needed; which ones depends on which types of CK are high, along with symptoms and medical history.

slides.title: Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; a fingerstick sample may be used in hospital  ·  Units: pg/mL, ng/L

What it is used for: Mainly used to help diagnose or rule out heart failure in a person with symptoms. Shortness of breath is the most common symptom of heart failure, but other conditions can cause it. If a short-of-breath person has normal BNP or NT-proBNP, heart failure can usually be ruled out; if levels are high, other tests are usually done to confirm.

slides.title: Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: In people already diagnosed with heart failure, the test may be used to find out how serious the condition is, predict the chance it will get worse, and check whether worsening symptoms mean the heart failure has worsened. In certain cases it is also used to monitor heart health after a heart attack or with unstable angina.

Ordered with symptoms that could mean heart failure: shortness of breath; swelling in the abdomen, feet, legs and/or neck veins; fatigue and general weakness; coughing; inability to sleep lying flat; needing to urinate a lot, especially at night; loss of appetite and nausea.

slides.title: Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: Heart failure is diagnosed from medical history, a physical exam and test results. Blood tests include BNP, whose level rises during heart failure; blood tests also show how well the liver and kidneys work. Imaging such as echocardiography measures how well the heart pumps (the ejection fraction).

Physiology: Natriuretic peptides are proteins made by the heart and blood vessels. BNP is a hormone the heart releases into the blood when it is working harder than normal to pump. BNP tells blood vessels to widen and the kidneys to get rid of water and salt in urine, lowering blood pressure and the amount of blood the heart must pump, which eases its workload. “Brain” is in its name because that is where it was first discovered.

slides.title: Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)
slides.eyebrow: Cardiac markers · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: NT-proBNP is the “ingredient” protein from which the BNP hormone is made; like BNP, more of it is made when the heart has to work harder. Some BNP and NT-proBNP in the blood is normal; levels higher than normal for age and sex may be a sign of heart failure. The provider decides which of the two to test.

slides.title: Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)
bullets: High: Higher than normal BNP or NT-proBNP means there could be heart failure; other heart tests are usually ordered to make a final diagnosis. In most cases, the higher the result, the more serious the heart failure may be.

High: BNP and NT-proBNP can also be raised by other conditions: kidney failure, other types of heart disease (affecting the heart valves or heart muscle) and certain lung disorders, including pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension. That is why medical history matters in deciding whether a high result means heart failure.

slides.title: Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Blood is usually taken from a vein in the arm; in hospital a fingerstick may be used, which gives quicker results. No special preparation is needed.

Interferences: With obesity, weight may affect accuracy and make levels lower than they really are. So if heart failure is suspected, other heart tests may be done even when BNP or NT-proBNP is normal.

Limitations: A BNP or NT-proBNP test alone cannot diagnose the cause of symptoms. What a result means depends on age, sex, medical and family history and other tests; a normal result means heart failure is unlikely, and other tests may be ordered to find the cause.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)

What it is used for: CK is most often used to help diagnose and monitor muscle injuries (from accidents, serious burns or extreme exercise) and muscle diseases such as muscular dystrophy, rhabdomyolysis and myositis.

In certain cases CK may help diagnose a heart attack, but troponin testing is used more often because it is better at finding heart muscle damage. After a stroke, CK may be measured to find out how severe it was and help predict the chance of another stroke.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Testing may be needed with symptoms of a muscle disorder (muscle pain or cramps, weakness, balance problems, numbness or tingling, dark urine, swollen legs or feet), after injuries that crushed or tore muscles or serious burns, when taking medicines that may damage muscle such as statins, or after a stroke or traumatic brain injury.

Physiology: Creatine kinase (CK, also called creatine phosphokinase, CPK) is an enzyme that helps make energy. Most of it is in skeletal muscle, with some in heart muscle and small amounts in the brain; normal muscle wear releases a little CK into the blood, while damage to muscle, heart or brain releases larger amounts.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
bullets: High: A higher-than-normal CK usually means some type of muscle damage. CK may not peak until up to two days after certain injuries, so repeat tests may be done; levels that stay high or keep rising may mean ongoing muscle damage.

High: A CK isoenzyme test helps show where CK comes from: high CK-MM most likely reflects skeletal muscle damage (disease, injury, medicines or recent intense exercise), and high CK-MB most likely heart muscle damage (heart attack, myocarditis), although a blood clot in the lung, heart surgery, congestive heart failure, hypothyroidism and kidney failure can also raise it. High CK-BB may mean a stroke or brain injury, or a condition affecting smooth muscle.

slides.title: Creatine kinase (CK)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, but to help make results accurate the provider may ask the patient to avoid intense exercise and alcohol for a few days before the test.

Limitations: Normal CK levels for a person depend on age, sex and race, muscle mass and physical activity. A CK result cannot show where the damage is or what is causing it, so symptoms and medical history are considered.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood; in certain cases cerebrospinal, peritoneal or pleural fluid

What it is used for: LDH is mainly used to check for tissue damage. It may help diagnose or monitor diseases of the blood (including anemia), liver, lungs, kidneys, heart (including heart attack), pancreas, brain and spinal cord, and help monitor conditions that may worsen over time, such as muscular dystrophy and HIV.

It may also help diagnose certain severe infections, show how serious some cancers are (multiple myeloma, lymphoma, leukemia, testicular cancer, melanoma) and check whether treatment for certain cancers is working.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: LDH (lactate, or lactic acid, dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that helps cells make energy and is found in almost all tissues, with the largest amounts in muscles, liver, kidneys and red blood cells. When disease or injury damages these tissues, the cells release LDH into the blood or other body fluids.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
cols: In general, higher-than-normal LDH usually means some type of tissue damage, usually from disease, infection or injury; more tests may be needed to diagnose the condition.

Lower-than-normal LDH is uncommon and usually not considered a health problem. Taking large amounts of vitamin C or vitamin E, or the rare genetic disorder lactate dehydrogenase deficiency, may cause low levels.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for an LDH blood test. For other fluids (cerebrospinal fluid by lumbar puncture, chest fluid by thoracentesis, abdominal fluid by paracentesis) the provider explains how to prepare.

Interferences: A high LDH does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: intense exercise and certain medicines, including aspirin, can raise it. LDH can also be high if many red blood cells broke open while the sample was collected and tested (hemolysis).

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Limitations: An LDH test alone cannot show what is damaging tissues or where the damage is, so it is usually done with other tests. The meaning of a result depends on why the test was done, the symptoms and other test results.
If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test, which measures five forms of LDH, may be ordered to help find the type and location of the damaged tissue and how serious the damage is.

slides.title: Heart attack (suspected myocardial infarction)
bullets: An emergency: the most common first test is an EKG (within minutes of arrival). Dying heart muscle cells release proteins into the blood; blood tests are often repeated to check for changes over time.

slides.title: Heart attack (suspected myocardial infarction)
rows: Troponin leaks into the blood when heart muscle is damaged; the main heart attack test, usually done with an EKG.
High CK-MB most likely comes from heart muscle damage, but troponin is better for finding a heart attack.

slides.title: Heart attack (suspected myocardial infarction)
rows: If the first result is normal, it is usually repeated within 12 hours; if high, two or more times over about 24 hours. The rise and peak help estimate the damage.

slides.title: Heart attack (suspected myocardial infarction)
rows: Heart muscle damage; very high levels most often mean a heart attack — judged with symptoms, EKG and other tests.
Troponin normal 12 hours after symptoms began
Other causes: unstable angina, arrhythmia, heart failure, valve disease, myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, chronic kidney disease, prolonged intense exercise and others.

slides.title: Heart failure
bullets: Diagnosis is based on medical history, a physical exam and tests: along with blood tests, ejection fraction (usually by echocardiography) and an EKG are assessed.

slides.title: Heart failure
rows: Helps diagnose or rule out heart failure in people with symptoms (especially shortness of breath); levels rise in heart failure.
Blood tests show how well the kidneys are working.
Blood tests show how well the liver is working.

slides.title: Heart failure
rows: In known heart failure — to assess severity, predict worsening and check whether new symptoms mean it is getting worse.

slides.title: Heart failure
rows: Heart failure is unlikely — another cause of symptoms is sought. Obesity can make levels read lower than they are.

Heart failure is possible; other heart tests are needed for a final diagnosis. Kidney failure, other heart disease and lung conditions (pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension) can also raise levels.

slides.title: Heart failure
rows: Heart failure with reduced (HFrEF) / mildly reduced (HFmrEF) / preserved (HFpEF) ejection fraction.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
bullets: High cholesterol is found from medical and family history, a physical exam and a blood test (lipid panel). Screening in healthy people: start at ages 9–11 and repeat every 5 years; every 5 years at 20–65 (every 1–2 years for men 45–65 and women 55–65); yearly after 65.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: The main source of cholesterol buildup and blockages in arteries; high LDL raises risk.
Helps decrease cholesterol blockages in arteries; low HDL is a concern.
High triglycerides may signal a higher risk of coronary heart disease.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: The main screening test is a lipid panel; fasting for 8–12 hours may be requested.
Total cholesterol minus HDL; may also be reported.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: Not part of a routine lipid panel; largely inherited and stable over life. May be ordered with a family history of stroke or early heart disease, or if family history is unknown.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: Higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease.
HDL < 40 mg/dL (≈1.0 mmol/L) in men or < 50 mg/dL (≈1.3 mmol/L) in women
May mean a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease; may lead to a statin prescription.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
bullets: Individual target levels are set by the clinician based on risk factors. mmol/L values are converted from mg/dL (approximate).

rows: >99th percentile URL; if the baseline is high, a >20% change in series – acute method-specific (ng/L)

slides.title: Many red blood cells broke open while a sample was collected, and LDH is high. How should this be viewed?
options: Broken red blood cells lower LDH, so the true value is even higher
Red blood cells contain a lot of LDH, and their breaking open during collection and testing can give a high LDH
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source names red blood cells among the richest sources of LDH and says LDH can be high in this situation.

Basis: MedlinePlus: LDH can be high if many red blood cells broke open when the sample was collected and tested.

slides.title: Why is an LDH test usually done together with other tests?
options: Because LDH is found only in the heart, and other tests are needed to check other organs
Because LDH cannot be measured in blood and is only estimated from other results
Because LDH alone cannot show what is damaging the tissue or where the damage is
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source gives this as the reason LDH is usually done with other tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: an LDH test alone cannot show the cause or location of damage, so it is usually done with other tests.

slides.title: Shortly after a crush injury, a patient's first CK is only slightly raised. Why might CK be repeated?
options: CK may not peak until up to two days after certain injuries, so repeat results show whether levels rise or fall
CK drops to zero right after injury, so the first result is always wrong
A single CK result shows exactly which muscle is injured
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source gives this as the reason more than one CK test may be done.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CK may not reach its highest level until up to two days after certain injuries, so more than one test may be done.

slides.title: For a suspected heart attack, what does the source say about CK?
options: Total CK is the preferred test
CK may help in certain cases, but troponin is used more often because it is better at finding heart muscle damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is what the source states.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CK may sometimes help diagnose a heart attack, but troponin is used more often because it is better at finding heart muscle damage.

slides.title: A patient with chest pain has a normal first troponin. According to the source, what usually happens next?
options: A heart attack is ruled out; no repeat is needed
It is usually repeated within the next 12 hours
Only total CK is measured instead of troponin
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Troponin rises about 2–3 hours after a heart attack begins, so a repeat test is needed.

Basis: Troponin usually rises about 2–3 hours after a heart attack begins; with a normal first result it is repeated within 12 hours.

Biochemical markers of myocardial infarction and risk factors?
bullets: 1. Myocardial infarction (4th universal definition): a rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit + clinical evidence of ischemia (symptoms, new ECG changes, pathological Q waves, imaging).
2. Troponin (I or T) is the main marker: rises at 3–4 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours, persists up to 7–14 days; with high-sensitivity troponin 1–3 hour algorithms.

slides.title: Biochemical markers of myocardial infarction and risk factors?
bullets: 3. Old markers: CK-MB – limited significance, only when troponin is unavailable (reinfarction); myoglobin – early but nonspecific; AST and LDH are no longer used in diagnosing MI.
4. Troponin also rises without infarction: myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, renal failure – dynamics and the clinical picture are important.

slides.title: Biochemical markers of myocardial infarction and risk factors?
bullets: 5. Risk factors and their laboratory reflection: dyslipidemia (LDL, non-HDL cholesterol, Lp(a)), diabetes (glucose, HbA1c), CKD (eGFR, albuminuria), inflammation (hs-CRP); non-modifiable – age, sex, heredity; smoking, hypertension, obesity.

slides.title: Markers of myocardial injury?
bullets: 1. Myocardial injury – troponin above the 99th percentile; with a rise/fall – acute; with added signs of ischemia – myocardial infarction.

2. Cardiac troponins I and T are cardiac-specific isoforms; high-sensitivity methods accurately measure low concentrations and give rapid rule-in/rule-out algorithms (0/1 or 0/2 hours); dynamics: when the baseline value is high, a change >20% is significant.
3. CK-MB – auxiliary (reinfarction, when troponin is unavailable), falsely raised in muscle injury; myoglobin – early, nonspecific.
4. Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) – wall stress, diagnosis and prognosis of heart failure; not for diagnosing MI.

slides.title: Markers of myocardial injury?
bullets: 5. Causes of troponin rise without infarction (myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, renal failure, arrhythmias, cardiac surgery) – clinical interpretation is needed.
